officials.close: **Which re-reads the saints.** This archive noted this morning that nine of the twelve children born to Valentino and Ursula at Rijeka between 1794 and 1805 carry *Nepomucena* or *Nepomuc*, and read it as Habsburg dynastic piety. That is half of it. **John of Nepomuk is the saint invoked against drowning** — the patron of bridges, and of men whose work is on the water. In a harbour master's town, a family that names nine children for him is not only being loyal. It is being careful.

southistria.note: Nine households of the name in one southern-Istrian parish across two hundred and twenty-four years, and **not one of them is joined to another by a record**. This is the archive's richest material and its emptiest tree. What follows is everything there is, in order, with every gap measured — because a web drawn honestly is worth more than a pedigree drawn hopefully. The place reads «Croazia, Austria» in the index on all of these; the parish is Svetvinčenat, resolved from the film, not from the place field.

cards.says: The household the archive has leant on hardest. Four children, and the godparents standing for them are Nadal, Batta, Andrea and Nardo De Franceschi — men of the same name in the same parish in the same decade.

rung.text: **Thirty-nine years above this household there is a baptism.** Elena di Franceschi, 21 December 1628, read on the page at Svetvinčenat — the earliest of the name anywhere in Istria that this archive has seen with its own eyes. She is not joined to anyone below her.

cards.says: Gasparo's three children begin eighteen years after Anto's last. A brother, a son, a cousin or a stranger — the register does not say.

rung.text: Anto's last child is 1674; Gasparo's first is 1692. **Nothing links them.** The one book that would — the Svetvinčenat marriage register — runs 1581–89 and 1622–23 and then jumps to 1762. The century that matters is not in it.

cards.says: Piero's household overlaps Gasparo's by fourteen years. Two men of the name fathering in one parish at one time is the ordinary shape of brothers, or of cousins.

rung.text: Overlapping households are **evidence of a family, not of a descent**. Two men fathering side by side cannot be put in sequence.

cards.says: Mattio, two children, sixteen years after Piero's last.

rung.text: No join shown.

cards.says: Nadal — the same forename as one of the godparents standing at Anto's baptisms sixty years earlier. A grandson's name, or a common name in a small parish.

rung.text: **Nadal is the only forename that recurs across the whole web.** It stands as a godparent in the 1660s and as a father in the 1730s. That is either the naming thread that ties the parish together, or it is two men who happened to share a saint's day. It is the single thing most worth testing.

cards.says: A century later, and the register has become tabular and Austrian. Six children to Antonio and Maria Bergamo — and the Bergamo family marries into this one twice.

rung.text: **Ninety years of silence** between Nadal's last child in 1735 and Antonio's first in 1825. This is where the web breaks in two.

cards.says: Francesca Defranceschi married Giovanni Bergamo and had seven children. This archive once printed her as the wife of Antonius Cerneca; that was wrong, and the error came from the tabular register's four parent columns being flattened into one list by the index. The correction stands.
Giacoma De Franceschi married Gio Battista Crosilla. Two children. A second Defranceschi daughter marrying out in the same six years as Francesca.
Joannes and Dominica Clagnan, four children, at the very end of the Austrian century. The last household of the name in this group.

rung.text: No join shown to anything above.

southistria.missing: **One book, and it is the one that is missing.** The Svetvinčenat marriage register covers 1581–1589 and 1622–1623, and then nothing until 1762. Every join on this page falls inside that hole. If a second copy of the seventeenth-century marriages survives — in the bishop's archive at Poreč, or among the Venetian provveditore's papers — this web becomes a tree in a week. If it does not, these nine households stay nine households, and the archive should go on saying so.

dalmatia.note: Eight households at Omiš between 1639 and 1887 — and one of them is another one, counted twice. They are set out in the order the index produced them. This is the parish evidence that sits underneath the family's own seventeen-generation chart, gathered independently of it; where the two touch is marked.

cards.says: The oldest Dalmatian household. Margarita baptised 4 March 1639. The index gives this couple a span of 1639 to 1867, which is not a marriage but a collision — a later record of the same two common names swept in with the earlier ones.
Franco and Lucretia, three children, one of them a **Zuanne born 24 May 1646** — the same forename as the head of the household above, in the same town in the same decade.

rung.text: Zuanne fathering from 1639 and a Zuanne born to Franco in 1646 are the naming pattern of **brothers, or of an uncle and his nephew**. It is the only thread between the two seventeenth-century Omiš households, and it is a forename.

cards.says: Gerolimo and Elena, two daughters, no year on either. Gerolimo is the name the nineteenth-century households give their first sons.

rung.text: **Two hundred and eight years with nothing in them.** Between Franco's children in 1646 and Francesco's first in 1854, this archive holds no Omiš household at all. The town's registers exist; they have not been read.

cards.says: **Seventeen children in twenty-three years** — the largest household in this archive. Giovanni Giuseppe Maria first, on 29 December 1854; the names run four and five deep, Rados Niccoló Maria, Giovanni Girolamo Andrea Felice.

**This is the household above, counted twice.** Six of these seven children are the same named individuals as in Francesco and Maria's list; the place differs only in language, Almissa being the Italian for Omiš; and the mother's surname differs by one letter, *De Caralipeo* against *De Caralipco*. **The seventh, Carlo Paolo Michele Maria, appears only here** — so the true household is not seventeen children but eighteen.

rung.text: **A duplicate, now identified.** The households list has carried this family twice since it was built, because the FamilySearch index writes the same town in two languages and two indexers read one surname differently. Flagged in the data; the merge is a separate job because the household ids are referenced elsewhere.

cards.says: Giovanni and Maria Ipsich, seven children, overlapping Francesco's household by fourteen years. Their first, Girolamo, was born and buried in 1860.

rung.text: **Three households fathering at Omiš at once** — Francesco from 1854, Giovanni from 1860, Niccoló and a second Giovanni from 1873 — and the first sons are called Girolamo and Niccoló, which are the names in the undated Gerolimo household. Brothers is the obvious reading. The Omiš marriage register would prove it.

cards.says: Niccoló and Teresa, five children, beginning with Riccardo Feligiano Maria on 9 June 1873.

A second Giovanni, with Giovanna Baucich — and **Baučić is the surname the family's own chart gives to Ivan's wife in the generation of 1829–1895.** The made chart and the parish index touch here, and this is the clearest place they do.

rung.text: Where «Rodoslovno stablo obitelji Franceschi» says *Ivan, 1829–1895, wife Ivanica Baučić*, the index says *Giovanni Franceschi × Giovanna Baucich, three children at Omiš 1873–1879*. Ivanica and Giovanna are the same name in two languages. **This is the join between the family's chart and the public record** — and it is an agreement, not a proof.

dalmatia.missing: **The Omiš marriage register.** Three men of the name fathering in the town at the same time in the 1860s and 70s, with first sons called Girolamo and Niccoló, is the shape of brothers — and one line in a marriage book would say whose sons they were. It would also test the chart's Ivan × Ivanica Baučić against the index's Giovanni × Giovanna Baucich, which is the single most useful thing anyone could do for this family. **And the two hundred and eight years between 1646 and 1854 are simply unread**, not lost.

peschle.note: Seven Peschle, one marriage into this family, and **exactly one stated filiation** among them. Drawn here because Lambertina is the mother of Carlo De Franceschi and therefore stands behind a great deal of what this archive believes about itself — and because her own parentage is blank. The households are in the order the records give them, with the join that everyone would like to make marked as the inference it is.

cards.says: The oldest Peschle this archive holds. One son recorded.

**The marriage that matters to this archive.** Lambertina Peschle married **Dominus Josephus de Franceschi at Gologorica on 3 February 1807**, second of ten children by that marriage being **Carlo**, born 17 October 1809 in house 17, class *Civilis* — the historian whose letter to Kobler is the family's own account of itself, and on whom half this site depends. She died at Gologorica on 16 July 1863. The 1826 status animarum of house 7 writes her *Lambertina*.

rung.text: **Is she Mathias's daughter?** She was born about 1786; he was born in 1756 and would have been thirty. The name is rare, the place is the same, and the generation is right. **Nothing says so** — her father is named in no record this archive has seen, and the Volosca registers have not been read.

cards.nlabel: ten children by the marriage · one named here

cards.says: **Paschalis Maria baptised 28 April 1832, and Carmina born and dead across 1832–33** — the two dates sit close enough that they may be twins, or a name re-used after a death, and the register would say which. Two of the children are recorded **at Fiume**, which is the move that matters: Volosca was Austrian, Fiume was **Hungarian crown land**, and the family crossed that line.

rung.text: Two Alexanders, eleven years apart: one born 1797 who married Anna Promagnoli, one born 1803 who is named as Mathias's son and married Franca Descovich. **Whether they are brothers, cousins, or one man the index has split is not shown by anything here.**

cards.says: Named in the index as **son of Mathias and Justina** — the only filiation anywhere in this group that is written down rather than guessed. No children recorded.

peschle.missing: **The Volosca registers.** Lambertina was born there about 1786 and married out of it in 1807; her baptism would name her father in one line and either close or break the link to Mathias. Volosca — Volosko, beside Opatija — was **Austrian Istria**, so its books are at Pazin or Rijeka, not in Hungarian paperwork. **And the Fiume side is the opposite case**: Pasqualina and Ercolano are recorded there, on Hungarian crown land, in exactly the jurisdiction this archive opened for the first time on 13 September 2026 and has barely begun to read.

dubrovnik.note: **Four records, and this archive said they were too thin to be anything.** That was wrong, and the reason it was wrong is instructive: read singly they are four unrelated Persich baptisms with a Defranceschi somewhere in the margin. Read together, and with the tabular-register rule applied to the first of them, **they are one household across forty-two years** — a Defranceschi daughter who married into Ragusa, and her three children.

cards.says: **The groom's parents.** The index files this as a birth and hangs four parent names on it — *Pietro Defranceschi, Marietta Defranceschi, Teresa Martechini, Antonio Persich*. Four names on one row is the signature of an **Austrian tabular marriage register**, whose printed columns run SPONSI, SPONSAE, GENITORES SPONSI, GENITORES SPONSAE, and which the index flattens into a single list. **This archive has been caught by that exact pattern twice before.** Read as a marriage it resolves cleanly: Matteo Persich, born 1829, son of Antonio Persich and Teresa Martecchini, marrying a daughter of Pietro Defranceschi.

**And the children carry the proof.** The first son is **Antonio** — his father's father. The daughter born 23 December 1863 is **Cattarina *Teresa* Vittoria Maria** — his father's mother. That is the ordinary Adriatic naming order, and it is independent support for reading the 1829 row as a marriage rather than a birth.

The index writes the mother *Maria* in 1853 and *Marietta* in 1863 and 1871, and the surname drifts from **Persich** to **Peršić** across the same eighteen years — one family, three spellings, as the century turns Croatian.

rung.text: **Marietta is the Defranceschi.** She is named as mother on all three baptisms and as a daughter of **Pietro Defranceschi** on the marriage row. Her own birth is in no record this archive holds, and neither is Pietro's — so the family that produced her is unplaced.

dubrovnik.missing:
**Who Pietro Defranceschi was, and what he was doing in Dubrovnik.** Marietta is the only Defranceschi in this group whose existence is certain, and she is documented entirely through her husband and her children. Her father is a name on one flattened index row.

Ragusa is neither Istria nor the Kvarner nor the Venetian Dalmatia of the Omiš chart — it was **its own republic until 1808**, with its own archive, and this archive has never searched it. The **Državni arhiv u Dubrovniku** holds the parish registers of the city and the republic's own records; nothing in this project has ever been asked of it.
